items.text: agree with Misti Y-- that some love Cirque but dislike Le Reve its diff discussion but whatever. for me theater and visual design are strongest part. scenery and decor are breathtaking start to finish and whole concept is beautiful and appealing. but doesnt translate well to live performance. storyline isnt that entertaining, and when i went to a show the stage malfunctioned repeatedly all evening, hard to stay engaged even during better scenes. got this used mechanical keyboard for 38 dollars. imo 38 is about what i got. maybe a bit more. space bar is a rattle city. every time you hit space it clacks like cutlery in a tray. i tune it out in the day but after midnight i just type around it. also E key repeats every now and then. meeting becomes meeeting. happens once every few paragraphs. rare enough i forget, frequent enough i reread everything before i send. i messaged seller to ask what switch. got tired of waiting and just got it anyway. answer came a week later. it was on my desk by then. browns. record. keeping it for comfort. little bump on each key partway down. fingers know a press registered without slamming to bottom. i can write a long email and wrists fine. laptop flat keys never managed that. thought about returning it. shipping would eat real chunk of what i paid. then im back on laptop. so it stays. rattle and all

remote work gets sold as the answer to everything. mentored 5 junior engineers for two years, so this feels overblown for any juniors still learning how to code. jrs don't need tickets or documentation or meeting. they need to sit in on design conversations. see how others debug issues. ask questions before they have hours of confusion. that kind of interaction happens organically in an office. for remote work, they need to know the right times to cut in, set up a call, and to explain a problem that they might not even fully understand yet. its a skill, and a tough one, to have before you have a chance to learn it. i've seen the feedback issues in remote work. short comments on code review can feel like the final word instead of a learning opportunity. also, it takes longer, so less momentum. the jrs i mentored typically improved faster if they had in person pairing, whiteboard sessions, etc. and had easy access to seniors. im not trying to push for offices or anti-flexibility. remote work can be great for self-driven devs. but for jrs, proximity is a booster that gives confidence, context, and instincts. sending jrs off with a laptop and a calendar can be a drag on junior development which can result in less good technical leadership in the future

3:17am. industrial mixer humming low and steady, felt it thru soles of elias boots. flour dust in air catching harsh fluorescent light like snow. sourdough loaves resting on wooden boards, crusts pale and soft before final bake. elias wiping hands on apron, fabric stiff with dried dough and sweat. went to front counter to check lock. ritual born of paranoia not necessity.

there it sat. The History of Salt. hardback, blue spine cracked near hinge. had appeared every Thursday for 6 weeks, always placed precisely on glass display case beside unsold cinnamon rolls. no library stamp indicated it belonged here. bakery was not a branch of municipal system. elias picked it up. cover felt cold. opened it expecting blank pages or a forgotten bookmark. instead a folded square of lined notebook paper slipped out, landed on counter with soft tap. unfolded it. handwriting was jagged pressed hard into fiber. You knead with your left hand dominant. Stop favoring the right. It ruins the tension. elias stared at words. mixer ticked over to next cycle. looked at his own hands, red knuckled and dusted white. closed book. placed it back on glass, aligning spine perfectly with edge. then turned off overhead light above display, leaving book in shadow

apple deserves mention here from my experience my school only let apple in for middle and high school. cost like double a pc. broke on a monthly basis. never dropped laptop, had to replace hard drive 5 times in 4 years, reinstalled OS lots of times. extreme case: friends macbook pro caught fire while watching a movie. smoke alarm went off. apple support wasnt diagnosing our problems just back it up, wipe it, restore files. same with iphones i had an original iphone and it was faulty frequently. now they put out new iphone every two months it seems, slight camera improvement. i will concede one qualified positive ipads are the best tablets now, but android tablets may catch up.

quick review of awakening at wynn vegas. its fine, not something i'd build a trip around. I've been to vegas constantly since i was a kid, saw tons of shows before 21. good baseline for what these productions can be.

good news is the circular stage. works well, any seat gets a decent view, rare for big theater shows. wynn/encore guests get $99 tickets, normally $125. nice deal.

some acts are impressive. performers strong as hell, aerialists, acrobats. but lots of feats feel like i've seen them done just as well in cirque du soleil.

bigger problem is story. its unclear, weak, or non existent. left not really knowing what its trying to say. also too much going on, too many visuals, moving pieces, wow attempts. more restrained would hit harder.

aside from a few cool stunts whole thing felt average. wasn't blown away, and no one i was with seemed overwhelmed either. few friends did enjoy it. if youve never seen it check it out, especially with the hotel deal. but i wouldn't see it again or pay full price a second time. it tries to be stereotypical huge flashy vegas spectacle. more equals better. more just meant messier for me.

so float valves control trough filling, its just a buoyant float hooked up to a valve. water level drops, float sinks, valve opens, water gets in. water rises, float rises too, valve closes gradually. at the set level it shuts off so filling stops. two normal reasons for overflow, debris or mineral buildup stops valve closing fully. also a misadjusted float set too high, so valve closes only after trough already overflowing.

siphon moves water between containers, its gravity and air pressure that pushes it over the hump. first you fill the tube with water so its a continuous column, no air. then gravity pulls water down the long side and its a bit of vacuum up top, low pressure. air pressure on top of the water pushes more up the short side.

the exit needs to be lower than the water surface in the container. driving force is weight difference of water column in both sides. if exit is higher or level with the source, gravity dont pull hard enough to compensate the lift on intake side. net pull is there only if the column in exit is heavier than the one rising.

air bubbles in tube break this whole thing, they break the column of water, molecules chain broken. air bubbles in means no suction, pressure equalized in tube with air outside, so no pressure difference to drive flow. siphon dies. then you have to re prime it, fill the tube with water.

I found the sourdough on its second rise again. its a thursday always, its on the flour bin always and there's always a copy of the count of monte cristo with the richmond public library stamp. I dont know how they get past the squeaky screen door without me hearing them, but honestly at 3am my brain is mostly yeast and caffeine anyway. tonight though a scrap of yellow legal paper was poking out of the top like a bookmark. I wiped my hands on my apron, left a ghosty white smudge on the dark cloth, and pulled it out. It said page 142, in frantic spiky handwriting, please. I think they're watching the drop box now. A cold draft swept through the kitchen, smelled of wet asphalt and rain about to hit. I looked at the darkened front windows, just saw my own tired reflection. didnt open the book. Carefully tucked the note back between pages, slid the novel into a brown pastry bag and folded the top down twice to seal it.

the flaws. space bar rattles on every press. not a click. hollow loose clatter. feels like a tray of cutlery being nudged. stopped noticing it during the day but at night it sounds way too loud. then the e key repeats itself, types meeting as meeeting. every few paragraphs. annoying enough i proofread.

seller was really slow to answer. asked what switches it was before buying. reply came a week later, keyboard already arrived. brown switches.

surprising part. the keys have a cushioned feel. satisfying. i write long emails, wrists don't complain. way better than the flat laptop keyboard i was using before.

i thought about shipping it back but the hassle wasn't worth it. so it stays on the desk. rattling. repeating. quietly earning its keep.

old registers are useful to historians for reconstructing daily life patterns. official narratives miss a lot. registers show up or absent, how regular, sometimes reasons for absence. so you can guess at seasonal labor, illness, bad weather, poverty, family stuff, migration, emergencies. also differences by gender, age, neighborhood, class, how education fit into work and household routines. look across years, you see schooling habits changing, public health. its a limitation though they only record what school chose to note. rarely explain kids experiences. absences misreported, incomplete or shaped by teacher assumptions. so most useful when compared with other sources.

217 every Thursday morning Mara finds this library book on the back step of the bakery. always same book, field guide to north american moths. county library sticker ghost pale on spine, some flour worked into the jacket as if the book had been helping her. she returned it twice. librarians were too polite with their smiles. by the third week she just kept it beside the rye starter, said nothing. tonight its raining, rain ticking on the alley door. ovens breathing. Mara shaping croissants, pressing butter into dough with her palms, then the latch click. tiny guilty click. no one there. just the book dry as bone on wet concrete. she wipes hands on apron, opens it. paper slip between luna moth and promethea pages, folded once. it says your window is the only light on this street. i read here until the first bus. im sorry about the crumbs. Mara looks at alley, dented milk crates, steam off the drains. city feels enormous for a sec then not. she tears corner off order pad writes cinnamon rolls come out at 405. puts note inside book. sets book on warm windowsill. unlocks back door.

did a classroom project on stability of folded cardboard bridges. used same cardboard same length and width where possible. short beam arch inspired and triangular fold designs. set between two supports, put weights on gradually to see them bend or tip or break. limited by how they were hand made, small number of trials, classroom conditions. so dont read the results like real engineering data. but the triangle folds seemed to hold weight steadier. so fold geometry kinda influences stability in model bridges.

found the book. *A Field Guide to Coastal Birds*. Steel table by back door under the bench where bread peels hang. Harbor Street branch stamp on cover, due date in March. Mail slot nailed shut years ago, but the delivery hatch beside it, flour man used it, never latched properly.

Eleven thursdays. Asked day staff, checked hatch for scratches. Once stayed past four, coat on, nothing. The book turned up between two and four and she was always at the ovens back to the door when it did.

Tonight a grocery receipt from Pell's was folded into the page on oystercatchers. Ink blotchy, someone pressed too hard.

I keep meaning to take this back to the library. Then I pass your door and there's the smell of bread and I put it down instead. I can stop if you want.

She smelled of salt she thought whoever it was, pages did.

Marguerite pulled a pencil from apron, wrote on back of receipt. Bring it Thursday. I'll have a roll. Tucked it in at the oystercatchers, set book on hatch ledge, warm roll in a paper bag beside it.

Toronto now, no more Hydro Ottawa, but I want to warn people, billing practices are scary. Had an account for a year when I was renting downtown. Moved in with my parents to do my MA and cancelled properly, paid off everything. But they kept taking money from my separate account at random times, over a year. Called them over and over, sent screenshots of the withdrawals, and reps kept saying account closed, no debits. Turns out they linked my bank info to my parents billing number because I said im moving back home. My parents didnt notice, they kept getting refunds from overpayments so credits seemed normal. Hours on the phone with multiple reps before a manager actually looked into it. Confirmed its their error, fixed it. But they initially refused a refund, offered apology only. Will never give bank info for auto debit again. Hydro Ottawa are careless with customers personal data, should really worry everyone.

at 340 am while second batch rye proofing marisol saw it again. library book on flour bin by back door, plastic jacket cold from alley. 4th thursday in a row. same book, field guide to night birds, stamped eastgate branch due 3 weeks ago. every time she carried it to drop box on way home. every thursday it came back, like the building itself borrowed it. wiped hands on apron, opened it. folded index card slipped out from barn owls page. "you leave the vent fan on. alley smells like bread til 5. i walk my mothers dog then cause she cant anymore. i keep forgetting to return this. maybe i keep not wanting to. —R" she read it twice while oven timer counted down. outside fan hummed pushing warm air into dark. she turned card over. used grease pencil for marking trays to write "rye's out at 415" then tore heel from yesterday's loaf, wrapped in wax paper, set book on top, propped back door open one inch.

thick skinned varieties are worse for this, the brantines. and they are splitting, im getting split in the brantines, so I know your frustration. so i got a big rain, big soaking rain on tuesday, and by thursday half my brandywines had let go. you can see the seam running down the side of the fruit. it is the old story of dry spell then sudden deluge. inside of the fruit takes water in faster than skin can stretch. and the sun golds are mostly holding out so far but I do have a few of them that look like they might follow.
can't really get around weather once it happens. the only thing that will help a bit is the 2 day schedule you're on, keeping it more on even keel. but it doesn't matter once the sky decides to let it all out in one go. you'll likely get a fair crop from the rest of the vines. just pick the split ones and put them to other use. but brantines are more of a headache. thick skin is a liability in a storm like this. may get better luck with sun golds if you can keep them from getting quite so much water in one go.

rooms feel stuffy even when its comfy but temp isnt everything. high humidity slows sweat evap from skin, air feels heavy and stale. low airflow too, no movement means co2 and odors and heat stick around you, dont disperse. bad venting traps that stuff in. AC cools the air but doesnt always fix humidity or circulation. opening window, fan, venting moves the air and lowers moisture.

Ive mentored 5 junior engineers for 2 years now and its not a win for everybody. Everyone says remote is great but the juniors really dont have it. They dont need tickets or docs or scheduled meetings what they need is being in on design arguments and watching someone else debug a nasty bug and getting answers before uncertainty snowballs. In an office you get all that for free. If you work from home, they have to figure out when to interrupt, get a call going, explain a problem they probably dont understand yet. That is very steep for someone who hasnt had a chance to learn. I have watched that setup screw up feedback. A short note on a code review reads like a final judgment. The lag on getting answers kills forward motion. The ones I worked with moved ahead much quicker when they could pair in person, work through things on a whiteboard, get hold of the seniors. None of this means scrap flexibility. It works fine if you can direct your own efforts. For beginners, being around other people is what gets them there. Its how they pick up confidence and context and judgment they will need. If you just hand a newcomer a laptop and a calendar, you will end up with weaker technical leadership down the road.

simple rain gauge just collects rain into opening of known area and gives you a depth, mm or inches. that depth is like how much water would cover flat ground if nothing drained, evaporated or soaked in. most gauges use a funnel with a wide opening feeding into a narrow measuring tube. same volume of water rises higher in a narrow tube so small amounts are easier to read. tube scale is marked to account for area ratio so readings still give true rainfall depth. wind is common source of error, gusts around the gauge can carry drops past the opening causing undercounting. evaporation or splashing before reading can also distort results.

Old school attendance registers are like a big gold mine for historians. These old logs tell us what life was like for people long gone, you can see patterns where seasons drive life. Attendance dips when flu hits or harvest time demands kids work instead of school. Its an important balance between going to school and making a living. Also if certain groups never showed up its probably cultural issues. But be careful. These records have problems. Teachers and headmasters could change the numbers to get funding or avoid questions from the authorities. So the data doesnt always match what was going on. Also they dont explain why a kid wasnt there, so researchers have to use other sources to fill the gaps. They are quantitative but you really need to check other evidence to get it right.

float valve connects trough to pressurized water line. the float is usually a plastic ball or block, it floats on water attached to a lever arm. when cattle drink level drops, float drops and tilts arm. pulls plunger or washer off valve seat and water flows in.
as water rises, float lifts with it. lever pushes plunger back on the seat, gradually narrows opening until flow stops at set level.
overflow happens for a few reasons, mostly when the washer is worn or dirty with debris so it cant seal on the seat. also happens if the float gets punctured and gets waterlogged so it doesnt rise enough to close the valve.
